spc.label: Statistical Process Monitoring (SPM)
spc.description: Control charts and statistical process monitoring methods.

scope.include: The paper proposes, extends, compares or applies a control chart or another procedure that monitors a process over time and signals when it changes.
scope.exclude: Control charts are only mentioned as background or used once as a minor tool; or 'control chart' means a flow diagram; or the paper is general time-series forecasting, anomaly detection or change-point analysis with no process-monitoring procedure.
scope.example_in: A nonparametric EWMA control chart for monitoring process location.
scope.example_out: A deep-learning forecasting model that cites control charts in its introduction.

narrative.summary: Say what is monitored, what kind of change the method detects, how the chart signals, and the main finding.
narrative.key_results: Report run-length or detection results with the shift sizes and in-control settings they refer to.
narrative.key_equations: The charting statistic, the control limits, and any run-length expression.
narrative.limitations_unstated: Consider effects of estimating parameters, autocorrelation, non-normality, which competing charts were left out, and how realistic the simulations are.
narrative.future_work_unstated: Consider relaxing assumptions, other data structures, diagnosis after a signal, software, and validation on real processes.

exp_design.label: Experimental Design (DOE)
exp_design.query: (ti:"experimental design" OR ti:"designed experiment" OR ti:"design of experiment" OR ti:"response surface" OR ti:"supersaturated design")

scope.include: The paper proposes, constructs, compares or studies how to choose the runs, points or allocations of an experiment (physical, computer or online), or analyses data from a designed experiment as its main subject.
scope.exclude: 'Experimental design' only names the setup section of an empirical study in another field; or a standard design is used once as a minor tool; or the paper is about observational data only.
scope.example_in: Construction of D-optimal split-plot designs for mixture experiments.
scope.example_out: A psychology study whose 'experimental design' section describes how participants were recruited.

narrative.summary: Say what is being designed, for which model and objective, how the design is constructed, and the main finding.
narrative.key_results: Report efficiency, run-size, estimation or prediction results, with the designs they are compared against.
narrative.key_equations: The assumed model, the design criterion, and the construction or algorithm.
narrative.limitations_unstated: Consider model misspecification, practicality of the run size, restrictions on randomization, computational cost, and how broadly the comparisons were made.
narrative.future_work_unstated: Consider other models or criteria, constraints met in practice, sequential use, software, and validation in real experiments.

reliability.label: Reliability Engineering
reliability.query: ((ti:reliability OR ti:degradation OR ti:maintenance OR ti:"remaining useful life" OR ti:"failure analysis") AND (cat:stat.ME OR cat:stat.AP OR cat:stat.ML))
reliability.description: Reliability, degradation and maintenance of engineered systems.

scope.include: The object of study is the failure, lifetime, degradation, maintenance or failure probability of engineered systems, components, structures or software.
scope.exclude: 'Reliable' or 'reliability' describes an estimator, a statistical method, a machine-learning prediction, a measurement instrument or a rating (for example inter-rater or test-retest reliability, or trustworthy AI); or 'degradation' or 'maintenance' refers to something other than engineered equipment.
scope.example_in: Bayesian analysis of Weibull-distributed bearing lifetimes under accelerated testing.
scope.example_out: Reliability of deep ensembles under distribution shift.

narrative.summary: Say what fails or degrades, what is modelled or optimized, what data are used, and the main finding.
narrative.key_results: Report estimation accuracy, prediction error, failure probability or cost results, with what they are compared against.
narrative.key_equations: The lifetime or degradation model, the likelihood or estimator, and any reliability or cost function.
narrative.limitations_unstated: Consider censoring and independence assumptions, extrapolation from accelerated conditions, validation on field data, and computational cost.
narrative.future_work_unstated: Consider other failure mechanisms, covariates and operating conditions, system-level effects, decision making, and validation on field data.

common_head.name: paper_type
common_head.label: Paper type
common_head.question: What kind of paper is this? Choose the one that best matches its main contribution.
values: Proposes a method that did not exist before.
Modifies or generalizes a named existing method.
Mainly compares existing methods or studies their properties.
Mainly applies existing methods to a specific problem.

common_tail.name: application_domain
common_tail.label: Application domain
common_tail.question: Which application area does the paper target? Use the area of its real data or the area it names as its target. If the method is general and only illustrated with simulated data, choose 'No specific application (general methodology)'.
values: Power, wind, oil and gas, water.
A general method with no target area.

common_tail.name: data_source
common_tail.label: Data used
common_tail.question: Which kinds of data does the paper analyse? Select every kind it actually uses.
values: Data from equipment or processes in use.
Real data: laboratory or designed test
Data from experiments or tests run for the study.
A named public dataset used by many papers.
Data generated by the authors from a model.

common_tail.name: code_used
common_tail.label: Computation performed
common_tail.question: Did the authors run computations (simulations, numerical studies or data analysis)?

common_tail.name: software_platform
common_tail.label: Software
common_tail.question: Which software or programming languages does the paper say it used? Select only those named in the paper.

common_tail.name: code_availability
common_tail.label: Code availability
common_tail.question: How can a reader obtain the authors' code? Choose the most accessible option the paper states. If computations were run but the paper does not say how to get the code, choose 'Not shared'.
values: A link to GitHub, GitLab, Zenodo, OSF or similar.
A package on CRAN, PyPI, Bioconductor or similar.
Code provided with the paper by the journal or arXiv.
A link to the authors' own site.
The paper says to contact the authors.
Code was used but no way to obtain it is given.

common_tail.name: software_urls
common_tail.label: Code links
common_tail.question: Every URL the paper gives for its code or software, copied exactly. Use an empty list if there are none.

spc.name: chart_family
spc.label: Data structure
spc.question: What kind of data does the proposed or evaluated chart monitor? Choose one.
values: One scalar quality characteristic at a time.
A vector of a few to tens of correlated characteristics.
The paper itself says the number of variables is large relative to the sample size, or uses sparsity or dimension reduction for that reason.
A relationship between a response and predictors (a curve or regression) observed at each time.
Whole curves or functions treated with functional data analysis.
Images, video, point clouds or spatial fields.
Networks or graphs observed over time.
The paper does not monitor a specific data structure, for example a broad review.

spc.name: chart_approach
spc.label: Approach
spc.question: Which of these features define the proposed or evaluated chart? Select a feature only if it appears in the title or abstract, or the charting statistic is built on it. Most papers have none or one.
values: In-control behaviour does not depend on the data distribution, for example rank or sign based.
The chart signals from a posterior or predictive distribution. Using a prior only in a simulation setting does not count.
Sampling interval, sample size or chart parameters change during monitoring.
Designed to resist outliers or contamination.
Chart parameters are chosen by minimizing cost.
Adjusts for case mix or covariates, common in healthcare.

spc.name: chart_statistic
spc.label: Charting statistic
spc.question: Which charting statistic does the paper propose or evaluate with its own results? The primary one is the statistic the paper is about. Competitors that appear only in a comparison table are not labels.
values: The signal uses only the current sample, whatever the type of limits.
Exponentially weighted moving average of a scalar.
Multivariate statistic using only the current sample.
Estimates when a change occurred as part of monitoring.
Charts applied to residuals of a fitted time-series or regression model.
A machine-learning model produces the monitoring statistic or the signal. Using machine learning only to diagnose causes after a signal does not count.

spc.name: phase
spc.label: Phase
spc.question: Which phase does the paper's own contribution address? Many Phase II papers use the words 'Phase I' because they take an in-control reference sample to estimate parameters or to set control limits. That is NOT Phase I. Decide by what the proposed or studied method does, and apply these tests in order, stopping at the first that fits. (1) The method needs no separate reference sample and updates its estimates with each new observation: 'Self-starting'. (2) The method itself analyses a fixed historical dataset, to find outliers or changes in it or to establish that the process was in control, and the paper proposes no online monitoring method: 'Phase I'. (3) The paper proposes one method of each kind, a retrospective one and an online one: 'Phase I and Phase II'. (4) The method monitors new observations as they arrive: 'Phase II'. This includes papers that estimate parameters from Phase I data, papers that split an example dataset into a Phase I part and a Phase II part, and papers that study how estimation error affects a chart. (5) Otherwise: 'Not applicable'. Examples: 'the first 150 observations are used as Phase I data to estimate the parameters and the rest are monitored' is Phase II. 'A chart is proposed to detect outliers in the historical sample' is Phase I.
values: Retrospective analysis of a fixed historical dataset.
The paper contributes a method for each phase.
Monitoring starts without a separate reference sample.
No phase applies, for example a broad review.

spc.name: phase_parameters
spc.label: In-control parameters
spc.question: How does the method treat the in-control parameters?
values: Parameters are estimated once from in-control data.
The paper studies how estimation error changes chart performance.
Estimates are updated as observations arrive.

spc.name: assumes_normality
spc.label: Assumes normality
spc.question: Does the proposed method assume normally distributed data?

spc.name: handles_autocorrelation
spc.label: Handles autocorrelation
spc.question: Is the method designed for autocorrelated (serially dependent) observations?

spc.name: handles_missing_data
spc.label: Handles missing data
spc.question: Is the method designed for missing observations or irregular sampling?

spc.name: evaluation_type
spc.label: How it is evaluated
spc.question: How does the paper evaluate chart performance? Select every approach it actually uses.
values: Run-length properties from a Markov chain approximation.
The paper evaluates no chart performance.

spc.name: performance_metrics
spc.label: Performance measures
spc.question: Which performance measures does the paper report in its own results?

spc.name: sample_size_requirements
spc.label: Reference sample guidance
spc.question: One or two sentences on what the paper says about how much in-control (reference) data is needed, with numbers if given. Write 'Not discussed' if the paper says nothing.

exp_design.name: design_type
exp_design.label: Design type
exp_design.question: Which type of experimental design does the paper propose, construct or evaluate with its own results? The primary one is the design the paper is about.
values: A subset of the factorial chosen by an aliasing structure.
Finds the few important factors among many, including Plackett-Burman.
Three-level screening designs that also estimate curvature.
Second-order designs such as central composite or Box-Behnken.
Factors are proportions that sum to one.
Hard-to-change factors, strip-plot, or other randomization restrictions.
Constructed by optimizing a criterion for a stated model.
Uses prior distributions or expected utility to choose the design.
Later runs depend on earlier responses.
Latin hypercube and related designs for simulators.
Points chosen one at a time by an acquisition function.
Online or field experiments comparing treatments.
Designs for clinical studies, including dose finding.
The paper analyses experiments but concerns no design type.

exp_design.name: design_objective
exp_design.label: Design objective
exp_design.question: What is the experiment designed to achieve? The primary one is the objective the paper states first or optimizes.
values: Finding factor settings that give the best response.
Estimating the effect of a treatment or intervention.
Insensitivity to noise factors or model misspecification.
Fewer runs or lower experimental cost.

exp_design.name: optimality_criterion
exp_design.label: Optimality criterion
exp_design.question: Which design criteria does the paper use to construct or compare designs? Select only criteria it actually computes.
values: Maximizes the determinant of the information matrix.
Minimizes the average variance of estimates.
Maximizes the smallest eigenvalue of the information matrix.
Minimizes the variance of chosen functions of the parameters.
A D-, A- or similar criterion averaged over a prior.
Expected reduction in entropy or a mutual-information utility.
Maximin, minimax, discrepancy or similar distance criteria.

exp_design.name: number_of_factors
exp_design.label: Number of factors
exp_design.question: A short phrase for how many factors the designs handle, for example '3 factors', '5 to 10 factors', 'up to 100 factors'. Write 'General' if the method is for any number, or 'Not specified'.

exp_design.name: evaluation_type
exp_design.label: How it is evaluated
exp_design.question: How does the paper evaluate its designs or methods? Select every approach it actually uses.
values: A real experiment was run or real data analysed.
Efficiencies or criteria computed for competing designs.

reliability.name: reliability_topic
reliability.label: Reliability topic
reliability.question: Which reliability topic does the paper address with its own results? The primary one is what the title and abstract are about.
values: Fitting or proposing distributions for time to failure.
Modelling gradual deterioration of a measured characteristic.
Predicting remaining useful life of a unit in service.
Detecting or classifying faults from condition data.
Accelerated life or degradation tests, test planning, demonstration tests.
Choosing when and how to inspect, repair or replace.
Reliability of systems of components or of networks.
Failure probability of structures from a limit-state function.
Repeated failures of the same unit.
Warranty claims or field return data.
FMEA, fault trees, root cause, risk assessment.

reliability.name: model_family
reliability.label: Model family
reliability.question: Which family of model does the paper propose or use for its main analysis?
values: Weibull, lognormal, exponential and similar, including regression on their parameters.
Wiener, gamma or inverse Gaussian processes.
Unit-specific degradation curves with random effects.
Poisson, renewal or other processes for repeated events.
Discrete states with transition rates, including semi-Markov.
Derived from the failure mechanism or a structural limit state.
Neural networks, tree ensembles and similar.
Gaussian process, polynomial chaos or other emulators of an expensive model.
Fault tree, Bayesian network or block diagram

reliability.name: inference_paradigm
reliability.label: Inference
reliability.question: How are the model's unknowns estimated?
values: Maximum likelihood, least squares, method of moments.
The paper develops or compares both.
Parameters are fitted by minimizing a loss, with no formal statistical inference.

reliability.name: computation_method
reliability.label: Computation
reliability.question: Which computational methods does the paper rely on for its main results?
values: EM, gradient or other optimization algorithms.

reliability.name: censoring
reliability.label: Censoring
reliability.question: Which kinds of incomplete lifetime observation does the paper handle? Select only kinds present in its data or model.
values: Some units had not failed when observation stopped.
Some failures happened before observation began.
Failures are known only to lie in an interval.
Units are observed only if their lifetime falls in a range.
The paper does not analyse lifetimes.

reliability.name: measurement_kind
reliability.label: Measurements
reliability.question: What is measured on the units under study? The primary one is the main input to the paper's model.
values: Repeated measurements of a deteriorating characteristic.
Vibration, temperature or other monitored signals.
Repeated failures or counts per unit.
Outputs of a simulator or limit-state function.

reliability.name: maintenance_policy
reliability.label: Maintenance policy
reliability.question: Which maintenance policies does the paper analyse or optimize? Most papers that are not about maintenance have none.
values: Replace at a given age or usage.
Act when a monitored condition crosses a threshold.
Act on a predicted future state or remaining life.
Combine actions across components or use downtime.
Repair restores the unit only partly.
The paper does not analyse maintenance.

reliability.name: evaluation_type
reliability.label: How it is evaluated
reliability.question: How does the paper evaluate its methods? Select every approach it actually uses.
values: Evaluated on a named public dataset.
A worked numerical example with assumed values.

narrative_fields.label: Future work stated by the authors
